title: The reefs that refuse to die
text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor yet shelter perhaps a quarter of all marine species — a concentration of life that puts rainforests to {{1}} (ASHAMED). Each reef is an animal collective: tiny polyps build the limestone architecture through a {{2}} (PARTNER) with microscopic algae that feed them by photosynthesis. Warm water destroys that arrangement. Stressed corals expel their algae and turn ghostly white, a phenomenon known as {{3}} (BLEACH), and if the heat persists the polyps starve. Events that once arrived decades apart are now measured in years, and the {{4}} (FREQUENT) of recent mass bleachings has stunned even pessimistic researchers. The scientific response has been strikingly {{5}} (INVENT). Divers raise corals in underwater nurseries, then cement fragments onto damaged reef in a technique known as coral gardening; elsewhere, teams are {{6}} (DELIBERATE) breeding hardier strains, cross-fertilising the survivors of warm-water events to speed up evolution. There is real ground for hope: some populations, notably in the Gulf of Aqaba, flourish in water that would bleach their distant {{7}} (RELATIVE). Even so, most researchers insist that restoration is {{8}} (ESSENCE) a holding action: replanted reefs buy decades, but only sharp cuts in emissions can secure the century.

gaps.explanation: 'puts rainforests to shame' — the noun of this family is shame.
'through a partnership with algae' — noun from partner.
'known as bleaching' — the gerund names the process.
'the frequency of recent bleachings' — noun from frequent.
'strikingly inventive' — full of inventions, from invent.
'would bleach their distant relatives' — plural noun from relative.
'restoration is essentially a holding action' — adverb from essence.
